content:
Allah, the polemic runs, is Baal under another name, or Hubal, the idol of the Kaaba. Robert Morey made the related "moon god" thesis popular in The Islamic Invasion (1992), and the claim still circulates in Christian apologetics.[1]

This article aims to provide context to that identification, insha'Allah, by reading the five sources it depends on: the Quran, the Arabic word, the earliest book on the Arabian idols, and two reports in Sahih al-Bukhari.

"There is nothing whatever like unto Him" (42:11). A god with a statue, a temple and a rival is, by the Quran's own measure, something other than Allah.

The Quran names Baal once, and only to condemn him. The prophet Elias asks his people: "Will ye call upon Baal and forsake the Best of Creators, Allah, your Lord and Cherisher and the Lord and Cherisher of your fathers of old?" (37:125 to 126).[2]

It is the Bible's own story. Elijah tells Israel on Mount Carmel, "If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him" (1 Kings 18:21, ESV).

Strength: firm. A scripture that tells men to forsake Baal for Allah does not teach that Allah is Baal.

In Arabic, as in Hebrew, ba'l is an ordinary word for a lord, an owner or a husband.[3] The Quran uses it of husbands: a wife who fears ill treatment "on her husband's part" (min ba'liha, 4:128), and Sarah's "this my husband" (ba'li, 11:72).

Hosea plays on the same double sense: "you will call me 'My Husband,' and no longer will you call me 'My Baal'" (Hosea 2:16, ESV).

A shared word proves nothing about a shared god. The Hebrew Bible itself calls a husband ba'al and condemns the Baals who stood in its people's shrines (Judges 2:13).

Hubal was a statue. Hisham ibn al-Kalbi (d. 819), in the earliest surviving book on the Arabian idols, describes it as red agate in human form, with its right hand broken off; Quraysh made it a hand of gold. Before it stood seven divining arrows.[4]

When the Prophet (peace be upon him) entered Mecca at the conquest, there were 360 idols around the Kaaba. He struck them with a stick in his hand, reciting, "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished" (17:81).[5]

Strength: firm. Allah's messenger broke the idols, Hubal's company among them. No one breaks the god he worships.

The sharpest witness comes from the battlefield. After Uhud, Abu Sufyan, then the leader of the pagans of Mecca, cried, "O Hubal, be high!" The Prophet told his companions to answer, "Allah is Higher and more Sublime."[6]

The enemy named his god and the Muslims named theirs, in a single exchange, as two and as rivals. The polemic asks the reader to believe that the two armies were shouting the same name.

The moon-god version fails on the Quran's first page of astronomy. "Adore not the sun and the moon, but adore Allah, Who created them" (41:37): the moon is a creature, and prostration to it is forbidden.

The pagans of Mecca knew Allah as the Creator before Islam and added partners to Him. We set out what they said in What the pagans of Mecca said about Allah, and the name itself in Who is Allah?

The bottom line

Five sources, and each sets Allah against the idol. The Quran tells men to forsake Baal for Allah. The Arabic word means a husband. Ibn al-Kalbi describes Hubal as a broken statue, the Prophet broke the idols, and at Uhud the two names were shouted against each other.

The identification has no text behind it. "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished" (17:81).

Notes

  1. Robert Morey, The Islamic Invasion: Confronting the World's Fastest Growing Religion (Eugene, OR: Harvest House, 1992).
  2. Quran 37:123 to 126, A. Yusuf Ali translation.
  3. Abul A'la Maududi on 37:125, and the Ma'arif al-Quran commentary on the same verse, both give the lexical sense of master, owner and husband.
  4. Hisham ibn al-Kalbi, The Book of Idols, trans. Nabih Amin Faris (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1952), the entry on Hubal. Ibn al-Kalbi credits Khuzayma ibn Mudrika with setting it up; Ibn Ishaq names Amr ibn Luhayy.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 4287, report of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud; the parallel in Sahih al-Bukhari 2478.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 4043, report of al-Bara' ibn Azib.
